nameStory: The 'cork' in Amur Corktree comes from its distinctive bark, which develops deep furrows and a spongy, cork-like texture as the tree ages. The 'Amur' part refers to the Amur River region where Russia meets China, part of this tree's native Asian homeland.
description: The Amur Corktree is a medium to large deciduous tree that can reach 40-50 feet tall with a broad, rounded crown. Despite its common name, it's actually a member of the citrus family, not related to true cork oak trees. This Asian native has compound leaves, small greenish flowers, and produces clusters of small black berries. It's considered an invasive species in New England and is listed as a noxious weed in Massachusetts.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - deeply furrowed, corky bark that feels spongy to the touch and has a yellowish inner layer visible in the deep grooves. On older trees, the ridges can be quite pronounced.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-13 leaflets arranged opposite each other along the stem, each leaflet oval-shaped with smooth edges. When crushed, the leaves release a citrusy, somewhat bitter smell.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small black berries about the size of peppercorns, clustered together and persisting into winter. They have a bitter taste and distinctive medicinal smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Develops a broad, spreading crown with thick, somewhat horizontal branching pattern. The trunk is often divided into multiple stems or has a distinctly buttressed base.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers appear in loose clusters in late spring to early summer. Male and female flowers typically grow on separate trees.

habitat: In New England, Amur Corktree is most commonly found in disturbed areas, urban parks, and along woodland edges where it has escaped cultivation. It tolerates a wide range of soil conditions and can establish in both sunny and partially shaded locations. You're most likely to encounter it near residential areas where it was originally planted as an ornamental tree.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring with their fresh green compound foliage. Small greenish flowers appear in loose clusters, though they're easily overlooked.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage provides dense shade with the distinctive compound leaves clearly visible. Female trees begin developing small green berries that will ripen later.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and the black berries ripen and become prominent in clusters. The corky bark becomes more noticeable as the tree goes dormant.
seasonality.winter: The deeply furrowed, corky bark is most obvious for identification. Black berry clusters often persist on branches, and the broad branching pattern is clearly visible.

funFact: This tree's inner bark produces a bright yellow dye and is one of the 50 fundamental herbs in traditional Chinese medicine, where it's called 'huang bo' - but ironically, the tree that gives us actual cork for wine bottles is completely unrelated and belongs to the oak family!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Black Walnut due to similar compound leaves, but Amur Corktree lacks the walnut's distinctive nuts and strong aromatic smell. Remember: 'Cork bark, citrus smell' for Amur Corktree versus 'Walnut fruit, pungent smell' for Black Walnut.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'cork tree,' this species is completely unrelated to the Cork Oak that produces wine bottle corks. The name confusion arises purely from the bark texture. Additionally, while it may seem like a harmless ornamental, it's actually an aggressive invader that can displace native forest species, which is why Massachusetts has banned its sale and planting.
compareHints: As the only Phellodendron species commonly found in New England, compare it instead to other members of the citrus family. Unlike native Prickly Ash, Amur Corktree lacks thorns and grows much larger. It also differs from other citrus relatives by having the distinctive deeply furrowed, corky bark and the ability to grow into a substantial shade tree rather than remaining shrubby.
